2.text: Cases of disproportionate ages of a married couple are by no means

3.text: common; for all marriages by exchange constitute only a fraction of all mar-

4.text: riages, and cases of disproportionate age occur only in a part of this group.

5.text: The terms of an exchange of women between families vary a good deal. The

6.text: exchange must not by any means be immediate; but a delay, even of several

7.text: years, is admissible. Sometimes, however, too much delay may lead to a

8.text: quarrel and change friendship to enmity.

9.text: Serving for a Wife. — The usual method of getting a bride is the so-

10.text: called ñaund˙oˊurg̣ɪn (literally, “for wife herdsman being;” i. e., the custom of

11.text: serving as a herdsman of the future father-in-law, in payment for the bride).

12.text: This institution, as its name indicates, evidently originated under the conditions

13.text: of nomadic life, and the necessity of having young men care for the reindeer-

14.text: herd. It reminds us of Laban, whose herd Jacob tended for years, first for

15.text: Leah, then for Rachel. The term applied to this custom is so firmly established

16.text: that it is used also even among the Maritime Chukchee, though they have

17.text: no herds, and the bridegroom simply lives in the house of the girl’s father

18.text: and works for him during a certain period.

19.text: Among the Reindeer Chukchee the term has acquired a broader meaning,

20.text: and is applied to all marriages in which the young man obtains his bride, not

21.text: through his family connections, but exclusively through his own efforts.

22.text: Before I take up the discussion of marriages concluded through service,

23.text: I must say a few words about those more romantic marriages in which a

24.text: young man obtains his bride, not through serving for her, but through braving

25.text: dangers and overcoming, enemies and competitors.

26.text: Marriages of this kind are very popular in Chukchee tales. Many of

27.text: these tales describe with vivid and picturesque detail how a man leaves his

28.text: own country and goes to a distant land in search of a bride, and what ad-

29.text: ventures he encounters. Some tales begin with a description of a single man

30.text: who lives quite by himself, and who has never seen any other human being,

31.text: particularly a woman. In another country lives a woman who has never seen

32.text: a man. Both feel a peculiar desire, which they do not understand. When

33.text: they meet, they do not know how to make love. This gives place to ridic-

34.text: ulous and obscene details. At last they learn by experience, and become

35.text: husband and wife. Other tales describe the adventures of a young man who

36.text: secures his bride right in the middle of a hostile camp or village.

37.text: In these tales much attention is given to the description of the bride,

38.text: which is made in two different ways. In one type of story, the bride is always

39.text: part in the holy act; but immediately all the people let go, and the bell fell to the ground. They were all

40.text: guilty of this sin. At this time this tale is obsolete. Some similar cases occur also among the Chukchee, but

41.text: the people talk about them not without derision. Thus, when I was travelling on the Wolverene River, I was

42.text: told that one Yeˊtɪläqäi was living with the wife of his minor son Atkaiˊñau. The people laughed at him, and

43.text: gave him a nick-name, ɪntaˊɪrɪnkên (“[of the] daughter-in-law [a] fond [one]”). This is not considered to be

44.text: proper, while group-marriages between a woman and men of her age are customary.
